nameStory: The name 'cobia' comes from the Spanish word 'cobo,' though the exact origin is unclear. This fish has collected quite a collection of nicknames over the years, including black salmon, ling, and even 'prodigal son' - perhaps because like the biblical character, it shows up unexpectedly when you least expect it!
description: The cobia is a large, powerful marine fish that looks somewhat like a cross between a shark and a remora (sucker fish). These sleek predators can grow quite large, often reaching 3-4 feet in length, with a distinctive elongated body and broad, flattened head. They're primarily tropical and subtropical fish, making them very rare visitors to New England waters - you'd be extremely lucky to spot one of these wanderers this far north.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Long, torpedo-shaped body with a distinctly flattened, broad head that feels almost shark-like when viewed from above

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark brown to black on top with lighter sides, often showing distinct horizontal stripes along the body that create a banded appearance

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Very distinctive first dorsal fin made up of 7-9 short, separate spines that stick up like a punk rock mohawk

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large terminal mouth (opens at the front of the head) with a slightly protruding lower jaw, giving it a determined, predatory expression

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Substantial fish typically 2-4 feet long in New England sightings, with a hefty, muscular feel - much larger than most fish you'd normally see inshore

habitat: In New England, cobia would most likely be encountered in warm coastal waters during the hottest part of summer, often around offshore structures, wrecks, or following larger marine animals. They prefer open water but may venture into large bays and harbors when water temperatures are at their peak.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be present as waters are still too cool for this warm-water species.
seasonality.summer: Your only realistic chance of seeing a cobia in New England - look during the hottest weeks when ocean temperatures peak, typically July through early August.
seasonality.fall: Possible in early fall during unusually warm years, but any individuals would be heading south as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Not present - these fish follow warm waters south well before New England's winter chill sets in.

funFact: Cobia have been observed following sharks, rays, and even sea turtles around the ocean, picking up scraps and small fish stirred up by their larger companions - like underwater dogs hoping for dropped treats!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its many common names, cobia is not actually related to salmon, cod, or any of the other fish its nicknames suggest - it's in its own unique family and is the only species of its kind in the world.
compareHints: Cobia is the sole member of its family Rachycentridae, making it truly one-of-a-kind. The closest comparison would be to jacks and pompanos (family Carangidae), but cobia's flattened head, separate dorsal spines, and overall body proportions make it unmistakable once you know what to look for.
